text: 📖 The story of the Syamantaka jewel
In the Yadava clan there were two brothers, Satrajit and Prasena.
Satrajit worshipped Surya, the Sun god, with great devotion.
Pleased with his devotion, Surya one day gave him a divine gem called the Syamantaka mani.
That jewel was said to hold great power.
Wherever it stayed, wealth and wellbeing followed.
Every day it gave a great measure of gold as well.
But there was one rule — whoever wore it had to remain clean and disciplined.
One day, as Satrajit came along the streets of Dwaraka wearing the jewel at his neck, the people who saw its blaze thought Surya himself was coming.
Sri Krishna, learning about the jewel, felt: “A gem this powerful would serve the people and the kingdom best if it stayed with King Ugrasena.”
But Satrajit, on hearing this, gave the jewel to his younger brother Prasena instead.
One day Prasena went hunting in the forest wearing the Syamantaka jewel at his neck.
There a lion attacked and killed him.
Then Jambavanta slew that lion.
Seeing the Syamantaka jewel beside the lion, he carried it to his cave and gave it to his little son as a plaything.
When Prasena did not return, Satrajit grew anxious.
And since the Syamantaka jewel he carried was missing too, he suspected: “It must be Krishna who killed Prasena for the jewel.”
That word spread through all of Dwaraka.
With blame falling on him for a wrong he had not done, Sri Krishna resolved to find out the truth.
Taking a few men with him, he went into the forest and searched for Prasena's trail.
There Prasena's body was found — and beside it, the pawprints of a lion.
Following them, he found the lion lying dead.
From there another set of footprints led to a cave.
Sri Krishna went into that cave alone.
There he saw a small boy playing with the Syamantaka jewel — his elder sister Jambavati beside him.
Just then Jambavanta arrived.
Thinking Krishna had come to take the jewel away, he rose to fight him.
Between the two a fierce battle raged for twenty-one days.
At last, one thing became clear to Jambavanta.
He realised that a man who could fight him this many days was no ordinary man.
The Lord he had once served as Sri Rama had now come as Sri Krishna — knowing this, he bowed to him.
Begging forgiveness for his mistake, he gave the Syamantaka jewel to Sri Krishna.
He also gave his daughter Jambavati — who had admired Sri Krishna from the moment she saw him — to him in marriage.
Sri Krishna returned to Dwaraka with the Syamantaka jewel.
When Satrajit learned the truth of what had happened, he was deeply pained.
He begged forgiveness for having blamed Sri Krishna without cause.
He gave his daughter Satyabhama to Sri Krishna in marriage.
He wished to give the Syamantaka jewel to Krishna as well.
But Sri Krishna did not take the jewel.
“It is yours,” he said, and gave it back to Satrajit.
Some time later, while Sri Krishna was away from Dwaraka, another incident took place.
Listening to the words of a few who were already unhappy over Satyabhama's marriage, Shatadhanva killed Satrajit and carried off the Syamantaka jewel.
He then left the jewel hidden with Akrura.
When Sri Krishna came to know of this, he returned, consoled Satyabhama, and with Balarama went after Shatadhanva.
In the end Sri Krishna caught Shatadhanva and slew him.
But search as he might, the Syamantaka jewel was nowhere on him.
With that, doubt rose even in Balarama.
“You found the jewel yourself.
Perhaps you have hidden it without telling me,” he said, suspecting Sri Krishna, and went away from there.
Though he had done no wrong at all, blame had come upon Sri Krishna yet again.
Why does this keep happening, one after another?
— Sri Krishna wondered.
Then Narada Maharshi told him the real reason.
🌙 The story of Vinayaka and the moon
It was the story of how the moon had laughed at Lord Vinayaka — and of the curse Mother Parvati gave him for it.
Narada told Sri Krishna what it means to see the moon on Bhadrapada Shukla Chavithi, and explained: “You too might have seen the moon that day.
That is why blame after blame has come upon you for wrongs you never did.”
Then Sri Krishna remembered that he had indeed seen the moon on Bhadrapada Shukla Chavithi.
So he prayed to Vinayaka.
Vinayaka appeared before him and blessed him: the blames that had come upon Sri Krishna would fall away.
Then Sri Krishna asked one thing: “If this could happen even to me, what of the ordinary people who look at the moon unknowingly?”
Then Vinayaka gave a boon to everyone.
He gave this boon: whoever sees the moon on Vinayaka Chavithi day, knowingly or unknowingly, will suffer no undeserved blame if they worship Vinayaka and listen to this story of the Syamantaka jewel.
Afterwards Akrura returned to Dwaraka.
The truth that the Syamantaka jewel had been with him all along became known to everyone.
With that, the doubts that had fallen on Sri Krishna were cleared away completely.
The story tells that while the Syamantaka jewel remained with Akrura, he used the wealth it brought for good works.
🙏 The shloka to say if you see the moon by mistake
simhah prasenam avadhit
simho jambavata hatah |
sukumaraka ma rodih
tava hy esha syamantakah ||
🙏 The counsel Suta Maharshi gave Dharmaraja at the end
Having told this whole story, Suta Maharshi counselled Dharmaraja: “You too keep the Sri Vinayaka vratam with devotion.
Your obstacles will fall away, and victory will come.”
Dharmaraja duly worshipped Vinayaka and kept the vratam.
In time he overcame his troubles and won back his kingdom.
So the Sri Varasiddhi Vinayaka vratam — which removes obstacles and grants success — has come down through the generations.
🙏 Om Gam Ganapataye Namah
🙏 Victory to Sri Varasiddhi Vinayaka Swami
